## Methods

Phage Mu preparation, genomic DNA isolation, and SMRT Sequencing
Two E. coli strains carrying phage Mu lysogen were obtained from Prof. Stan Hattman and were used to produce Mu phages. Of the two strains, one contains the Mu lysogen (denoted as ER3153; genotype: sup mcrA thi hsdR mcrB zzz::Mu(Cts62)) which produces the Mu phage with the native 6-NcmdA DNA modification phenotype, and the other has a mutant Mu lysogen which produces Mu phages without 6-NcmdA DNA modification but canonical 2´-deoxyadenosine phenotype (denoted as ER3154; genotype: sup mcrA thi hsdR mcrB zzz::Mu(Cts62 mom)).
A heat-shock procedure was performed to induce the production of Mu phage from the lysogen. LB medium was inoculated with the phage lysogen strain from an overnight culture and was incubated at 37 °C with agitation until an OD reading of ~1. The culture was then incubated at 45 °C for 30 minutes and then again at 37 °C with agitation. Phage were harvested when the culture appeared translucent (cells lysed), a process that normally takes about 1.5 – 3 h after heat-shock. The phage lysate solution was then centrifuged at 10000 rcf x g at 4 °C for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected. The phage was then concentrated first by precipitation in a solution of 10% (w/v) poly(ethylene glycol) average MW 8 kDa and 1 M NaCl, followed by pelleting by centrifugation, and finally resuspension in a buffer composed of 50 mM Tris-HCl 7.5, 10 mM MgCl and 75 mM NaCl. The phage solution was stored at 4 °C in the dark. A previously published protocol was followed to extract and purify phage genomic DNA90.
Genomic DNA isolated from phage Mu was used to prepare the single-molecular real-time (SMRT) sequencing libraries. SMRT sequencing reads were analyzed using SMRT Analysis software and pipelines from SMRT Link webtool (version 10.2.0) hosted by Pacific Biosciences. SMRT sequencing raw CCS reads were processed to generate HiFi reads in which the output sequences were used for the de novo assembly of the genome using MEGAHIT assembler software (version 1.2.9) 91. The longest assembled output sequence was used as the reference for subsequent SMRT Analyses steps. Base modification detection and motif analysis were performed with the same SMRT Link version. To detect the base modifications, the Base Modification Analysis application was used to first map the raw reads to the assembled genome and the mapped reads were analyzed further to extract the inter-pulse duration (IPD) kinetics information collected during sequencing course and processed for all pulses aligned to each position in the reference sequence using an in silico kinetic reference and a t-test based kinetic score detection of modified base positions. The per-base IPD ratio mapped outputs were further used to extract the modification motifs. The top three identified modification motif sequences were extracted separately and the sequences for each motif string were used to generate sequence logo by using WebLogo 3 webtool (version 3.7). See Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 2.

DNA Substrates
Biotinylated DNA substrates were prepared by digesting  DNA (NEB) with MseI (NEB) as described32,33,90. Digested  DNA was backfilled with 50 µM Biotin-16-(5-aminoallyl)-dUTP (Jena Bioscience) using Klenow Fragment (3´→5´ exo-) (NEB). Empty plasmids of pUC19 (NEB) and pET28a were used as supplied. Double-stranded DNA oligomers were obtained by heating a 1:1 mix of complementary oligonucleotides at 90 °C for 5 min and annealing by gradual cooling to the room temperature for 30 min. Duplexes were stored at -20 °C until use. Mu 34-mer was resuspended in Duplex Buffer (IDT), complementary strands were mixed in equimoloar ratios, and annealed by heating at 95 °C for 2 minutes and cooling to room temperature over a linear gradient. The 3 kbp substrates were amplified with a standard dNTP mix, 15N -dATP (Cambridge Isotope Laboratories), dGTP, dTTP, and dCTP, or 6-15N-dATP, dGTP, dTTP, and dCTP. 6-15N-dA (Toronto Research Chemicals) was chemically phosphorylated (see Supplemental Methods). See Supplementary Table 1 for sequences.

Recombinant protein expression of Mom

Cells were incubated with 140 rpm shaking for 18-20 h at 25 °C. Cells were then collected by centrifugation, washed with PBS (pH 7.4) and stored at -20 °C.

1, Why Ac-CoA is not an optimal donor for modifying the dA,
Acetyl-CoA cannot be the group donor as it does not contain the necessary complement of atoms matching the hypermodification. Multiple chemical steps and extraordinary chemistry would need to be invoked in order to break bonds in Ac-CoA in such a way as to carve out a nitrogen group. Previously published hypotheses regarding Mom function posited multiple enzymatic steps including radical chemistry and amidation to produce the mature modification. Here we show a single enzyme in the absence of any aminotransferase can accomplish the momylation reaction.
However, we do appreciate the discussion from Reviewer 3 and Reviewer 2 above about what is driving co-substrate specificity for GNAT enzymes. As discussed above in our Response to Reviewer 2, an acetyl group does not have the correct stoichiometry for reconstituting 6-NcmdA in a single transfer step. We also emphasize again here that this is an interesting and open question in the field that we are hopeful will become clearer over time. To date, there are multiple examples of distinct GNAT family members that have convergently evolved the ability to utilize aminoacylated tRNAs as group donors targeting diverse substrates (discussed and referenced in the main text). We present here a new example of a GNAT family member following this pattern and, significantly, the first known and shown in vitro to modify dsDNA. There is a possibility that another GNAT enzyme might exist which uses acetyl-CoA to modify the N6 position of dA within the DNA duplex. This enzyme has not been discovered to our knowledge. In our response to Review 2 above, we discuss TcmA, the enzyme that acetylates N4 of cytidine in tRNA, so it would be mechanistically plausible from an enzyme standpoint for similar chemistry to take place in DNA. However, we note that ac4C is unpaired in tRNA and in the context of DNA, an acetyl group could cause steric clash with the cognate base-pair. Such a steric clash is mitigated in 6-NcmdA through greater degrees of freedom afforded by an additional carbon between N6 of dA and the planar carbonyl of the carbamoyl moiety. Another factor that needs to be considered here is the microbial arms race between bacteria and their viruses. The modification ac4C has been reported to undergo spontaneous deacetylation in vitro at room temperature at neutral pH21. Considering the extreme selection pressure phage are under by their hosts, a potentially more labile modification may not be advantageous for protecting against host defenses (e.g. restriction enzymes).
why mom prefers dsDNA over ssDNA,
The preference for dsDNA is not unusual or unexpected. Mu is a dsDNA phage, and Mom is post-replicatively active (see main text). Many phage-encoded DNA modifying enzymes operate on dsDNA post-replicatively (e.g. T4-BGT). Furthermore, ssDNA would be only transiently available at the replication fork. As with understanding co-substrate preference, understanding the structural basis for the substrate preference can be explored in future work.
why mom prefers SAS sequence motif,
This is also an open-ended question that has both mechanistic and biological aspects. We do not yet know what amino acids at the protein-DNA interface dictate sequence specificity. There is also a biological “why” here. Does the SAS sequence allow for maximum protection against multiple endonuclease-based antiphage systems targeting different sequences? Or does SAS sequence preference also impact the biology of the host, perhaps by overlapping with dcm? Does the SAS sequence allow for sufficient modification (~15-20%) of the Mu genome without negatively impacting the biophysical properties of the gDNA? These questions, while fascinating, are beyond the scope of the work presented here and do not impact our findings.

All structures reported in the current manuscript meet the ORCA criteria for convergence (as noted in the manuscript). Specifically, these are: All minima and saddle points/transition states met the ORCA criteria for convergence of geometry optimizations, i.e root mean square gradient (RMSG) below 1 * 10-4 Eh/au, maximum gradient (MaxG) below 3 * 10-4 Eh/au, energy change (TolE) below 5 * 10-6 Eh, RMS displacement (RMSD) below 2 * 10-3 au, and maximum displacement (MaxD) below 4 * 10-3 au, where Eh is 1 Hartree (~627.5 kcal/mol), and au is one atomic unit (one Bohr, 0.52 Å).
